title: My paid-off semi-D has been empty for ten years. Should I keep it, sell it or refinance?
excerpt: A debt-free 56-year-old has a paid-off semi-D worth about RM1.7 million sitting empty. Sean lays out three paths, rent and refinance, sell, or stay debt-free, and says the choice depends on what he wants.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K is 56 and a partner in a stable company he has run for 18 years. He lives in a fully paid townhouse and also owns a semi-detached house in Shah Alam worth about RM1.7 million, which has been empty for ten years with no loan. He doesn't want to move into it or spend time keeping it up.
question.text: Should he keep the semi-D and hope it appreciates, or sell it and buy condos for rental income?

answer.quote: It's more of a self-awareness question.
answer.summary: Either works; it depends on whether he wants to stay debt-free, or grow richer for himself or his family. Sean's own choice would be to fix it up, rent it out, refinance only as far as the rent covers the new instalment, and use the cash to buy more. If he thinks the area has peaked, selling and reinvesting is sensible too.

reasons.title: Refinancing turns idle value into cash
reasons.body: Renting the house out and borrowing against it, only up to what the rent can repay, keeps the house break-even while releasing cash for other purchases. Banks lend to about 70, so at 56 he has about 14 years of loan tenure.

reasons.title: Short loans need more cash down
reasons.body: With a 10- to 14-year loan, rent rarely covers the instalment, so any new purchase needs a large down payment, or he must accept topping up every month.

reasons.title: Sell if the area has peaked
reasons.body: When a neighbourhood already has its schools, hospital, commercial areas and transport and no land left, prices tend to flatten. Selling then and moving the money into higher-yield property can make sense.

reasons.title: Debt-free is already a strong position
reasons.body: With two paid-off homes, a business and savings, he is financially free. Staying as he is is fine; the real danger is a bad business venture, such as friends asking him to invest RM300,000.

actions: Decide what the money is for: comfort, a hobby, charity, your children's education or a larger legacy.
Ask agents what the semi-D would rent for once cleaned up, and what similar houses sell for.
If you refinance, borrow only what the rent can repay, and keep your own savings untouched.
If you sell, consider whether the area has any growth left, then reinvest in units whose rent covers their costs.
Turn down requests to put money into friends' businesses you don't understand.
caveat: Sean didn't know the rent the house could fetch or whether the asker has children, both of which change the answer. He also notes that, unlike in a gated estate, an empty landed house affects its neighbours.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #223. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in September 2023.
